name: Jamal Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers or government. This is confidential. Tell me about a usual working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the drill rig on the lower benches, beginning with a walk-round and a radio check. The hard part is knowing when a small vibration means the ground has changed. I like teaching new operators that a careful stop is part of a good shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew I can live with a tool that tidies the service forms. I operate the drilling rig, and a program won't feel the vibration through the seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our income is sound and we have enough saved to carry a long interruption. I still don't want the office measuring a shift by how quickly we fill boxes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the same rig roster and compare any automatic service entries against my maintenance notebook each Friday. I'd continue setting aside part of the higher shift pay for the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. The usual early start is tiring, but my job and pay look steady in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did your notebook catch recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hose was rubbing against the guard although the pressure reading was normal. I marked it after the evening wash and maintenance replaced it before the next shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let your children try the software?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let them use it for a school project if their teacher wanted. At home, my partner Samira and I still check what comes out of any screen.

say: I'd say **service forms** can be quicker if operators still check the machine before signing.
I'd remind the crew a **drill rig** tells the driver things through vibration that a form may miss.
think: Our **income** and savings make this a comfortable picture for the mortgage household.
I dislike **box counting** if management begins judging a shift only by how fast forms are completed.
do: Keep the **rig roster** and compare automatic service entries with my maintenance notebook every Friday.
Continue putting part of my **shift pay** against the mortgage on the usual payment date.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, despite ordinary fatigue from early starts.
S0.quote: A hose was rubbing against the guard although the pressure reading was normal.
fieldNote: He accepts a faster **form** once checked against physical inspection, consistent with using AI only when it proves useful.
Strong **savings** and steady pay support his calm mood; he still guards against management mistaking form speed for good work.

steps.text: Keep rig roster and compare automatic service entries with the maintenance notebook

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the office to show us how the new ordering and planning tools work before changing the drill schedule. Robots may come later, so today's issue for us is whether a bad plan sends equipment to the wrong face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could see fewer jobs for people who prepare schedules, and that troubles me. My own drilling shifts should remain, but I want the crew trained on a tool before anyone calls it safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to watch a trial of the planning screen on our own benches. In the first year I'd learn its route alerts from a trained operator and bring any wrong locations to the shift safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about colleagues and mistakes, while expecting my wage to hold. I don't mind learning after someone has shown that it works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the trial convincing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let it plan a wet-weather shift and compare its routes with the drivers' radio reports. A polished dry-day run proves very little at our mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you bring to the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with my colleague Pavel, who covers the far bench and knows where a drill can turn safely. We would bring the route printout, not just a complaint.

say: I'd ask the **office** to demonstrate planning tools before they change the drill schedule.
I'd say slower **robot** rollout leaves our immediate risk in poor routes and lost planning jobs.
think: I expect some **scheduling jobs** to shrink, although my own drilling shifts look secure for now.
I need a **proven trial** before trusting new route alerts with heavy equipment.
do: Watch a **wet-weather trial** of the planning screen on our own benches this year.
Learn **route alerts** from an experienced operator and bring wrong locations to the shift safety meeting.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and unsafe routes, with my own income still appearing steady.
S1.quote: A polished dry-day run proves very little at our mine.
fieldNote: He wants a **wet-weather trial**, which fits his habit of adopting technology once it works in real conditions.
His worry for **schedulers** differs from his income outlook; slower robots leave his rig shifts likely to continue.

steps.text: Watch a wet-weather planning screen trial on our benches
Learn route alerts from an experienced operator during the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the 2028 thinking change may overhaul plans and service records before our rig is touched. If hands-on robots work by about 2031, management needs to tell us what machines it actually plans to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is tight for a driver to prove another trade. Our savings cover many months, and there are other mines around, but losing my higher pay would force a hard look at the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written equipment timetable this winter and call two nearby mines about drilling vacancies. If our shifts fall after 2028, I'd apply for those posts; in the first year I'd cancel the planned workshop extension at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, because I can imagine a real pay cut before the children finish school. I have options, but none is as solid as today's roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the extension would you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We were going to add a covered bay for my old motorbike and tools. The workshop can wait; our mortgage cannot. The house works without the new bay, and the money can stay ready for payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take any vacancy you found?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask about the roster and safety record before moving. My partner Samira has a job nearby, so I would not move the whole family for a vague offer.

say: I'd separate **2028** changes to plans and records from possible hands-on robot drilling around **2031**.
I'd ask management for a **purchase timetable** before deciding how exposed our operator shifts are.
think: Losing my **higher pay** would strain the mortgage even with savings lasting many months.
Other **mines** offer possible work, but I will check roster and safety before counting any vacancy as secure.
do: Request the **equipment timetable** and call two nearby mines about actual drilling vacancies this winter.
Apply if **shifts fall** after 2028, and cancel the planned home workshop extension in the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about the household wage before the children finish school, though savings and local jobs allow choices.
S2.quote: The workshop can wait; our mortgage cannot. The house works without the new bay, and the money can stay ready for payments.
fieldNote: He keeps the **family home** as his base, since his partner works nearby and a vacancy elsewhere is uncertain.
Cancelling the **workshop extension** is concrete spending restraint; money merely held ready is not counted as new saving.

steps.text: Call two nearby mines about drilling vacancies and apply if shifts fall
Cancel the planned home workshop extension in the first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our supervisor the 2031 planning change gives us time to test the reports, while robot rigs around 2034 are a separate decision. We should ask for a demonstration on broken ground before buying the promises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to prepare a second skill, though I can't assume every miner will get a place. My mortgage would be smaller by then if we keep our current payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid maintenance apprenticeship if the mine offers one by next year, even if it means some evening study. I'd keep the rig shifts during training and review the family budget once the course hours are real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the eventual rig jobs, but I can act while my pay is still strong. A known apprenticeship feels much safer than an unknown job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of maintenance interests you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already help trace hydraulic leaks after shutdown, though a qualified fitter makes the repair. I'd like to learn maintenance work properly rather than guess around a high-pressure line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship isn't offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my drilling certificate current and ask nearby mines whether they fund one. I wouldn't pay a private school upfront on the strength of an advertisement.

say: I'd distinguish **2031** planning changes from possible robot rigs around **2034**.
I'd ask for a **broken-ground demonstration** before believing that machines can handle our difficult benches.
think: Five years might let me learn **maintenance**, but an apprenticeship place is not guaranteed.
Our **mortgage** should ease if we keep paying it, giving the family room to consider a different role.
do: Take a **paid maintenance apprenticeship** if the mine offers a place by next year while keeping rig shifts.
Review the **family budget** when course hours are known, and maintain the drilling certificate if no place appears.
feel: **Uneasy** about future rig work, with enough runway to try a paid apprenticeship if one exists.
S3.quote: I'd like to learn maintenance work properly rather than guess around a high-pressure line.
fieldNote: His interest in **maintenance** grows from hydraulic checks he already assists, giving the course a credible job path.
The apprenticeship remains **conditional** on a paid place; he avoids paying for an unproven private course.

steps.text: Take paid maintenance apprenticeship if mine offers a place by next year
Keep rig shifts while attending any paid maintenance course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2036 could put the planning desk on a new footing, and about 2039 is when robots might do the hands-on drilling. A decade lets a family make choices without a rushed sale or move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 when thinking AI arrives and 56 when robot rigs might compete. I may still want to work then, and I expect an apprenticeship record would matter more than a last-minute course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine this year to let me mentor a new driller on inspections and keep our mortgage payments steady. If the mine opens a recognised maintenance apprenticeship in the next few years, I'd start it; nearer 2036 I'd decide whether to work on repairs or stay on the rig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough to plan. I don't need to gamble the family's savings while the years are still on our side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the trainee first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a new driller how to stop and check the hydraulic line before touching a suspected leak. A trainee's first good habit can save a lot of trouble later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for a trainer post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without a firm offer and a conversation with my partner Samira about the children's plans. We have other mines close enough to check first.

say: I'd mark **2036** for planning work and possible robot drilling around **2039**.
I'd tell families the **decade** gives room to choose a path without rushing to sell or move.
think: At **53 and 56**, I may still want to work, so a record of training matters more than a rushed course.
Our **savings** need not be gambled early while nearby mines and steady payments give us choices.
do: Ask to **mentor** a new driller on inspections this year while keeping regular mortgage payments.
Start a **recognised maintenance apprenticeship** if the mine opens one in the next few years.
feel: **Calm** about the long runway, with no need to risk the household reserve now.
S4.quote: A trainee's first good habit can save a lot of trouble later.
fieldNote: He uses the long horizon to **mentor** and perhaps learn maintenance, without claiming he would retire by 2039.
He says a move would require a **firm offer** and family discussion; nearby mines make immediate relocation unnecessary.

steps.text: Mentor a new driller on hydraulic inspections this year
Start recognised maintenance apprenticeship if mine opens one

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the gap to possible robot drilling around 2031 is short, and our mortgage depends on my higher pay. A dated equipment plan and funded maintenance apprenticeships would help us make a choice while my roster still holds.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how a new operator learns to stop when a screen says to carry on. That judgment needs time beside an experienced worker, even if the software is clever.

headlineQuote: I don't need to gamble the family's savings while the years are still on our side.
portrait: **Jamal**, 43, drives a mine drill rig; his vocational training and higher pay support a partner, two children and a mortgage.
He has substantial **savings** and nearby mines, and uses AI occasionally after seeing a tool work under real site conditions.
He remains **calm** under a plateau, then watches planning jobs and unsafe routes under slower disruption.
The short **2028-to-2031** gap makes him anxious about lost drilling pay, while longer horizons allow a conditional maintenance apprenticeship.
He values **mentoring** and wants paid training with a real place before risking the family reserve or leaving their town.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings possible robot drilling around 2031, leaving little time to protect the higher wage that pays his mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A dated **equipment plan** and funded maintenance apprenticeships would let him choose a path while his drilling roster holds.
